House GOP Saves Hegseth—for Now—and Picks Jordan to Lead
 
Plus, lawmakers want tighter export controls in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, and allies worry over Washington’s pivot on European security
 
 
JIM LO SCALZO/EPA/SHUTTERSTOCK
 

Good morning. Tuesday showcased tense secret votes and even more tense public votes. But at the end of it all, House Republicans saved a cabinet secretary from impeachment and picked Rep. Jim Jordan (R., Ohio) to lead them heading into what will likely be a wild final two years of President Trump’s second term.

 

The House GOP rescue of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was no small feat, and Republicans mostly united to block an impeachment vote from one of their own, Rep. Thomas Massie (R., Ky.). In January, when Democrats have a mega-majority, they will have more than enough votes to impeach Hegseth if they so choose, but the Pentagon chief’s deliverance Tuesday—one week after Republicans’ midterms shellacking—served to pause an avalanche of losing that some Republicans felt was only getting worse.

 

In addition, by picking Jordan to serve as House minority leader next year (in a secret ballot, he bested Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana), they have selected someone skilled at congressional investigations and messaging.

 

These will be really important skills in a moment when Democrats might overwhelm the system with investigations of, well, nearly everything the Trump administration does.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Trump’s arch: Nine Kennedy family members joined legal efforts to block the construction of President Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

 

Trump’s Wednesday: It is Veterans Day. President Trump and first lady Melania Trump are scheduled to participate in a wreath-laying ceremony at 11 a.m. ET at Arlington National Cemetery, where the president is then set to make remarks at 11:30 a.m.

What I’m Following

 
 
REUTERS
 

The Jensen Huang scandal revives push for chip restrictions on Capitol Hill. Lawmakers are demanding tighter restrictions on chip exports following Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, a business partner suspected of being a Chinese intelligence source. The push threatens to cost Nvidia and other semiconductor companies billions of dollars in revenue.

 

U.S. overture to Russia on European security sparks alarm. The Trump administration is pushing to renegotiate pan-European security alongside ceasefire talks to help end the war in Ukraine. The White House’s approach is causing alarm in many European governments, which believe Russia’s real goal is to rebuild a sphere of influence in Europe’s east, giving it a say over other countries’ defense and security policies.

 

John Thune won another term as GOP Senate leader, but there was grumbling. The South Dakota senator won by acclamation, but ahead of the vote, Sen. Ron Johnson (R., Wis.) and a half-dozen other Republicans had argued that the party needed to do a self-evaluation before sticking with the same leadership team. “That kind of defeat demands change,” said Johnson, referring to the midterms. But, he added, “That’s part of our problem: Who would want the job?”

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• A senior U.S. Army soldier who was assigned to a NATO rapid reaction command structure in the U.K. has been arrested on allegations of spying for Russia.

 

• A county-by-county look at how the blue wave touched nearly every part of America.

 

• Stubborn inflation raises pressure on the Federal Reserve for a December rate increase.

 

• The SEC obtained penalties last year totaling $1.1 billion, the lowest tally in nearly two decades.

 

• Proponents of Proposition 40 in California have already floated putting another wealth tax on the ballot in 2028.
